validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: I re-derived the root cause myself rather than taking it from either document: on main, activating the skip link leaves document.activeElement on BODY with hash #main set and the viewport scrolled, because src/web/pages.js:77 emits <main id="main"> with no tabindex. Applying tabindex="-1" locally and re-driving headless Chromium moved activeElement to MAIN#main on all 25 route x state combinations, and the next Tab entered main wherever main has a control. I also re-measured the two things the critique called blocking and confirmed both: on every ?state=error route focus is pre-positioned on the retry button inside main by src/web/client.js:36-40, so the proposal's 'press Tab once' procedure cannot reach the skip link there and its own two-Tab workaround does not work either; and the shells that wrap back to the top of the document are the ones whose main holds no focusable element, which is every route in the loading state plus more of the ideal/empty/partial shells than the proposal listed. The test-count error is arithmetic I re-confirmed against a 273-test baseline. What keeps this off a higher number: I verified one engine only, my attempt to exercise the JavaScript-disabled path did not actually disable the script so the 'works before hydration' claim is untested, screen-reader announcement is unverifiable in this pipeline, and re-activating the skip link when the hash is already #main I did not measure. None of those is load-bearing for the fix; all of them are things a person may want to look at.
validated_work_order.understanding: Issue #52 carries one QA finding from the review of PR #50: activating the skip link moves the viewport to #main but leaves document.activeElement on <body>, so the keyboard user is returned to the header the link promises to skip. I reproduced it before planning, as the ticket asks. The cause is a single missing attribute: src/web/pages.js:77 emits <main id="main"> with no tabindex, and a fragment link only transfers focus when its target is focusable, which <main> is not by default. src/web/pages.js:68 emits the link itself, a.skip-link[href="#main"], correctly. The remedy is tabindex="-1" on the landmark — programmatically focusable, still not in the tab sequence — which is the standard WCAG 2.4.1 bypass technique and needs no JavaScript. One existing test (test/web/pages.test.js:116) reaches into main with a regex that assumes the exact tag text and fails on the new attribute; it is part of this change. The diagnosis stands. What does not stand is the proposal's verification surface: two of its four acceptance criteria and one step of its QA script are unexecutable or false as written, so QA following them literally would report failures the change does not cause. Those are corrected below, and the wrap-around case is restated as a measured set rather than a remembered one.
validated_work_order.root_cause: main#main is emitted without tabindex, so it is not a focus target: HTMLElement.tabIndex reads -1 and getAttribute('tabindex') returns null. Per the HTML spec, following a same-document fragment link sets the sequential focus navigation starting point to the target but only moves focus if the target is focusable; a non-focusable target leaves document.activeElement on <body>. Where main contains no focusable element at all, the next Tab has nowhere to go and wraps back to the top of the document, re-entering the skip link and then the header. I measured on a seeded database which shells those are, and they are not the three routes the proposal names — see residual_risks for the measured set.
validated_work_order.approach:
Three edits to source, two test edits, no new file, no new dependency, no JavaScript.

1. src/web/pages.js:77 — emit `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">`. This is the whole behavioural fix: fragment navigation to a focusable target focuses it natively, in every browser, with and without the client script. tabindex="-1" is deliberate and not tabindex="0": the landmark must be programmatically focusable but must not join the tab sequence, or every page would gain a spurious stop before its real content.

2. src/web/styles.css, immediately above the existing `#main { ... }` rule — add a scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }`. With only the attribute, Chromium reports `main#main.matches(':focus-visible') === true` after the skip link is activated and paints the repository's global 2px accent outline (rgb(29, 95, 191)) around the entire 1100px main container, which at these scroll positions reads as two unexplained vertical bars at the viewport edges. The suppression is scoped to `#main:focus` only, so the skip link keeps its own focus style and every other focusable keeps the global ring. The file comment must say that the suppression works by ID specificity — `#main:focus` is 1,1,0 against the bare `:focus-visible` at src/web/styles.css:55 which is 0,1,0 — so that nobody later 'simplifies' it to `main:focus` and silently loses it. outline is not inherited, so no descendant of main is affected.

3. test/web/pages.test.js:116 — the existing heading-hierarchy test slices the document out of main with /<main id="main">([\s\S]*?)<\/main>/, which stops matching the moment a second attribute is on the tag. It fails today with `undefined !== 1` for all 25 route x state combinations. Capture the tag and its attributes instead of pinning the tag text, so the extraction does not depend on which attributes the landmark carries or in what order — the same decoupling #46/#51 applied to the h1 hook.

4. A new test in the same file pins the new invariant across the full route x state matrix, the way the h1 invariant is pinned: the skip link still targets #main, and main#main carries tabindex="-1". The assertions must be genuinely order- and insertion-independent: extract the tag once (/<main([^>]*)>/ and /<a([^>]*)>/) and assert /\bid="main"/ and /\btabindex="-1"/ against the captured attribute string, the shape already used by the .page-title coupling test at test/web/pages.test.js:1091-1093. Asserting the two attributes in one regex with `[^>]*` between them is not enough — it tolerates a third attribute but still fails on <main tabindex="-1" id="main">, which is a valid no-op refactor and would be reverted as a false regression. Pin that property explicitly, as the h1 matcher test at test/web/pages.test.js:145-152 does.

5. A second new test pins the stylesheet rule, matching /#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/ and asserting outline: none. This follows the precedent set two tickets ago for the .page-title rule at test/web/pages.test.js:1096-1102: asserting the stylesheet's own contents is convention-clean under .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and it makes AC-3's claim machine-checkable. Without it, the one line that suppresses a visible artefact can be deleted with a green suite.

I applied edits 1-3 locally and re-drove headless Chromium: activeElement becomes MAIN#main on all 25 route x state combinations, and the next Tab enters main on every shell that has a control there. Everything is reverted; the working tree is clean apart from this plan.

files.change: Line 77: `<main id="main">` becomes `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">` in layout(). The landmark is the skip link's target; without tabindex it is not focusable and the link only scrolls. Nothing else in layout() changes, and the emitted attribute is static markup, not user or store data, so it crosses no escaping boundary.
files.why: The root cause. One attribute, no JavaScript, native behaviour in every browser.

files.change: Add a scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }` rule with a comment, placed immediately above the existing `#main { max-width: 1100px; ... }` rule it belongs with. The comment must record two things: that the rule exists because focusing the whole main container paints the global accent ring around the entire 1100px box, which reads as two stray bars at the viewport edges; and that the suppression works by ID specificity (1,1,0 beating the bare `:focus-visible` at 0,1,0 on line 55), so lowering the selector to `main:focus` would silently lose it. `.skip-link:focus` (line 50) and the global `:focus-visible` rule (line 55) are untouched.
files.why: Verified in Chromium: with only the tabindex, main#main matches :focus-visible after activation and the global ring is painted around the whole container. The ring on a landmark communicates nothing a sighted user can act on; the skip link already showed its own visible focus at the moment of activation.

risks: The single existing test the change breaks, test/web/pages.test.js:116, fails on all 25 route x state combinations until its extraction stops pinning the tag text. I have run this: the failure is `undefined !== 1` from levelsOf(mainOf(html))[0], i.e. the extraction returns '' rather than the h1.

The CSS change suppresses a focus outline. It is scoped to `#main:focus` and does not touch `.skip-link:focus` or the global `:focus-visible` rule, and I confirmed the accent ring is still computed on a real control after the skip link, but it is the one line in this change a reviewer may reasonably challenge. The reasoning is in the file comment and in alternatives_considered; a reviewer who disagrees can drop that one rule at the cost of two visible bars per skip-link activation. A reviewer should also read the comment's specificity claim before accepting the rule, since the suppression silently stops working if the selector is ever lowered.

Only Chromium was available in this environment, so the fix is verified in one engine. tabindex="-1" on a fragment target is long-standing, specified behaviour and is the technique GOV.UK's template uses, so a second engine is expected to agree. The :focus-visible heuristic that motivates the CSS line is more engine-specific than the fix is: Firefox and WebKit may not paint the ring at all, which would make the rule inert there rather than wrong. Firefox and WebKit are the gap QA should close if it has them.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add a click handler in src/web/client.js that preventDefaults the skip link and calls document.getElementById('main').focus().
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Strictly worse for the same outcome. It makes the bypass depend on the deferred script having loaded and executed, so the failure mode returns on any slow parse, any CSP change, or a browser that blocks the script; the link would again silently only scroll. It needs preventDefault to suppress the browser's own fragment handling, so it also has to reproduce scrolling by hand, and it adds a second place that knows about the main landmark. The native remedy — tabindex="-1" on the target — is what the HTML spec already prescribes for fragment links to non-focusable targets, works before hydration, and is one attribute.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add the tabindex only, and leave the focus ring the browser paints around main.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is functional but visibly wrong, and I would rather not ship it. Chromium paints the repository's global 2px accent ring around the entire 1100px main container, which at these scroll positions reads as two unexplained vertical bars at the edges of the viewport. Nobody reads that as 'you are in main'. The scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }` rule is the one extra line that avoids shipping it, and it is the same thing GOV.UK's template does for its skip target. This is a judgement call, not a correctness one — a reviewer who prefers the visible ring can drop the rule without touching the fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Point the skip link at the page's <h1 data-testid="page-title"> instead of at <main>, and give the h1 tabindex="-1".
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Focus would land on a heading, not on the content region, so the bypass lands mid-landmark: screen reader users would hear the page title rather than main, and the next Tab would resume from inside the heading rather than from the top of the content. It also couples the bypass target to a styling-driven element that #46 and #51 have just spent two tickets decoupling from its class. No benefit to trade for that.

alternatives_considered.approach: Handle the wrap-around case at the same time, by making focus land on the first focusable element inside main when one exists.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The wrap is not a defect in the skip link. The shells that wrap contain no focusable element at all — the loading shells are skeletonRows, and the ideal and empty shells on three routes render panels and copy — so there is genuinely nothing for focus to reach, and wrapping to the top of the document is the correct behaviour when the next tab stop is behind you. Fixing it would mean changing page content, which is a product decision belonging in its own ticket. It is stated precisely in residual_risks rather than folded in here.

alternatives_considered.approach: Assert the new invariant with a single regex over the tag, e.g. /<main id="main"[^>]*tabindex="-1"/.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It reads as attribute-order independent and is not. `[^>]*` tolerates a third attribute interleaved between the two asserted ones but still fails on <main tabindex="-1" id="main"> — the same valid markup, emitted in the other order. A no-op refactor would then fail the regression lock and get reverted as a false regression, which is the exact trap the H1_HOOK matcher at test/web/pages.test.js:20-23 exists to avoid, and the currency #44 and #51 were filed to close. The assertions go against the captured attribute string instead, and the property is pinned explicitly.

assumptions: Chromium's behaviour on fragment navigation to a tabindex="-1" target is representative of the browsers QA drives. The spec rule is engine-independent and the technique is long-established, but I verified one engine only.

The route's debug stage will not conclude differently from this. Both the proposal and the critique reproduced the failure on the same tree, and so did I, so a disagreement at debug would be about the remedy rather than the fact of the bug.

docs/ui.md line 114 ('Every page is fully operable by keyboard: visible focus ring, logical tab order matching the region order') is a statement of intent that a landmark container is not a 'user interface component' for focus-ring purposes, so #main:focus needs no ring. This is the premise of the one CSS line; if a reviewer reads 2.4.7 more strictly, that line should be dropped and the bars accepted.

No test other than test/web/pages.test.js:116 depends on the exact text of the <main> tag. This is load-bearing — it is why edit 1 is expected to break exactly one test — and I did not take it on the grep alone: I applied the change and ran the suite, which produced exactly one failure, at that test. The grep and the run agree.

The focusable-element inventory in residual_risks holds for a seeded database, which is the state the QA script sets up. On an unseeded database the ideal states collapse toward the empty shells and the wrap set shifts. It is stated as a property of the shells that have no focusable content, not as a permanent route list, so it survives a reseed.
unknowns: Whether Firefox and WebKit are available anywhere in this pipeline. If QA only ever drives Chromium, the multi-engine gap never closes and AC-1/AC-2 rest on the spec plus Chromium.

Whether the pipeline's browser QA can disable scripting, so that the 'works before hydration' claim in alternatives_considered can actually be exercised. I tried and did not manage it, so the claim stands on the spec rather than on a measurement.

Whether re-activating the skip link in a document whose location.hash is already #main re-runs the focus fixup. Engine-dependent and unmeasured; it is a qa_script step rather than an acceptance criterion because I do not know the right answer to assert.

Whether focusing main#main actually announces the main landmark in a screen reader. This is the user benefit the change exists for and nothing in this pipeline can confirm it; the criteria here are all activeElement- and computed-style-based, and the announcement is carried in residual_risks rather than asserted.

Whether the Librarian intends .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md to record tabindex="-1" as part of the main#main hook contract. The existing line is still true as written, so nothing is broken either way, and that file is one this ticket may not change.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: The council did not agree, and the disagreement was worth having. Both documents agree on the diagnosis and on the remedy, and I confirmed both myself on the running app: tabindex="-1" on the landmark is the right fix, minimal, and its collateral damage is exactly the one test both documents name. Nothing argued for a different fix and I rejected none of the critique's substantive points. What the critique got right, and what changed the work order: the entire verification surface needed rewriting, not the plan's substance. Its two blocking findings both survived my own re-measurement. The error-state one is real and worse than a wording problem — src/web/client.js focuses the retry button inside main on load, so on all five error routes the proposal's 'press Tab once, press Enter' cannot be executed, and the workaround the proposal offered for exactly that case (two Tabs) does not work either. I checked the focus inventory route by route and state by state rather than accepting the critique's list, which is right in direction but still omits the two partial shells; the measured set is in residual_risks and AC-2 is scoped to the shells that actually have something to reach. On its own the critique called AC-2 false for /journal and /experiments in the loading state, which is true and is the case most likely to come back as a bug report after merge. Three further findings I accepted: the new test's advertised attribute-order independence is not achievable with the `[^>]*` technique the proposal prescribes — I confirmed the failure on <main tabindex="-1" id="main">, and the repo's own H1_HOOK precedent says the fix is to assert against the captured tag — the promised 273 is 275 once both new tests land, and I re-confirmed the 273 baseline myself; and the #main:focus rule should be pinned by a test, since this repository added exactly that kind of stylesheet assertion two tickets ago for the .page-title rule and the omission would let the one line that suppresses a visible artefact be deleted with a green suite. Two minor findings I accepted as written (AC-2 named the journal filter select as the landing target for /experiments, which actually lands on INPUT#composer-title; and the CSS comment should record that the suppression works by ID specificity, so nobody later lowers the selector and silently loses it). One finding I recorded as confirmed with no action, since the finding itself asks for none: the caller's grep is exhaustive — my own run of the suite after the change produced exactly one failure, which is the stronger form of that evidence anyway. What I rejected from the critique's edge-case list is the screen-reader criterion: it cannot be passed or failed by anything in this pipeline, so asserting it would buy a criterion nobody can check. It is in residual_risks, where QA will read it and know it is unverified. The proposal's own confidence of 92 was too high for a plan whose acceptance criteria are wrong in two places on 5 and 2 of 25 combinations respectively; mine is 85, and the reasons it is not higher — one engine, an unexercised JavaScript-disabled path, an unmeasured re-activation case, an unverifiable screen-reader claim — are all recorded.
residual_risks: The wrap-around set, measured on a seeded database and re-measured by the arbiter. These shells render no focusable element inside main, so after the skip link moves focus to MAIN#main the next Tab has nothing to reach and returns to the top of the document, where the header is re-entered. The set is: all five routes in the loading state (skeletonRows emits only <div class="skeleton">); / in ideal, empty and partial; /opportunities in ideal and partial; /approvals in ideal and empty. That is 12 of 25 shells, not the three routes the ticket named. QA should go here first, because it is the most likely thing to be reported as a bug after merge. It is correct behaviour given the content, it is a direct improvement on the pre-fix behaviour, and it is deliberately not fixed here — see out_of_scope.

approved_work_order.confidence_rationale: I re-derived the root cause myself rather than taking it from either document: on main, activating the skip link leaves document.activeElement on BODY with hash #main set and the viewport scrolled, because src/web/pages.js:77 emits <main id="main"> with no tabindex. Applying tabindex="-1" locally and re-driving headless Chromium moved activeElement to MAIN#main on all 25 route x state combinations, and the next Tab entered main wherever main has a control. I also re-measured the two things the critique called blocking and confirmed both: on every ?state=error route focus is pre-positioned on the retry button inside main by src/web/client.js:36-40, so the proposal's 'press Tab once' procedure cannot reach the skip link there and its own two-Tab workaround does not work either; and the shells that wrap back to the top of the document are the ones whose main holds no focusable element, which is every route in the loading state plus more of the ideal/empty/partial shells than the proposal listed. The test-count error is arithmetic I re-confirmed against a 273-test baseline. What keeps this off a higher number: I verified one engine only, my attempt to exercise the JavaScript-disabled path did not actually disable the script so the 'works before hydration' claim is untested, screen-reader announcement is unverifiable in this pipeline, and re-activating the skip link when the hash is already #main I did not measure. None of those is load-bearing for the fix; all of them are things a person may want to look at.
approved_work_order.understanding: Issue #52 carries one QA finding from the review of PR #50: activating the skip link moves the viewport to #main but leaves document.activeElement on <body>, so the keyboard user is returned to the header the link promises to skip. I reproduced it before planning, as the ticket asks. The cause is a single missing attribute: src/web/pages.js:77 emits <main id="main"> with no tabindex, and a fragment link only transfers focus when its target is focusable, which <main> is not by default. src/web/pages.js:68 emits the link itself, a.skip-link[href="#main"], correctly. The remedy is tabindex="-1" on the landmark — programmatically focusable, still not in the tab sequence — which is the standard WCAG 2.4.1 bypass technique and needs no JavaScript. One existing test (test/web/pages.test.js:116) reaches into main with a regex that assumes the exact tag text and fails on the new attribute; it is part of this change. The diagnosis stands. What does not stand is the proposal's verification surface: two of its four acceptance criteria and one step of its QA script are unexecutable or false as written, so QA following them literally would report failures the change does not cause. Those are corrected below, and the wrap-around case is restated as a measured set rather than a remembered one.
approved_work_order.root_cause: main#main is emitted without tabindex, so it is not a focus target: HTMLElement.tabIndex reads -1 and getAttribute('tabindex') returns null. Per the HTML spec, following a same-document fragment link sets the sequential focus navigation starting point to the target but only moves focus if the target is focusable; a non-focusable target leaves document.activeElement on <body>. Where main contains no focusable element at all, the next Tab has nowhere to go and wraps back to the top of the document, re-entering the skip link and then the header. I measured on a seeded database which shells those are, and they are not the three routes the proposal names — see residual_risks for the measured set.
approved_work_order.approach:
Three edits to source, two test edits, no new file, no new dependency, no JavaScript.

1. src/web/pages.js:77 — emit `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">`. This is the whole behavioural fix: fragment navigation to a focusable target focuses it natively, in every browser, with and without the client script. tabindex="-1" is deliberate and not tabindex="0": the landmark must be programmatically focusable but must not join the tab sequence, or every page would gain a spurious stop before its real content.

2. src/web/styles.css, immediately above the existing `#main { ... }` rule — add a scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }`. With only the attribute, Chromium reports `main#main.matches(':focus-visible') === true` after the skip link is activated and paints the repository's global 2px accent outline (rgb(29, 95, 191)) around the entire 1100px main container, which at these scroll positions reads as two unexplained vertical bars at the viewport edges. The suppression is scoped to `#main:focus` only, so the skip link keeps its own focus style and every other focusable keeps the global ring. The file comment must say that the suppression works by ID specificity — `#main:focus` is 1,1,0 against the bare `:focus-visible` at src/web/styles.css:55 which is 0,1,0 — so that nobody later 'simplifies' it to `main:focus` and silently loses it. outline is not inherited, so no descendant of main is affected.

3. test/web/pages.test.js:116 — the existing heading-hierarchy test slices the document out of main with /<main id="main">([\s\S]*?)<\/main>/, which stops matching the moment a second attribute is on the tag. It fails today with `undefined !== 1` for all 25 route x state combinations. Capture the tag and its attributes instead of pinning the tag text, so the extraction does not depend on which attributes the landmark carries or in what order — the same decoupling #46/#51 applied to the h1 hook.

4. A new test in the same file pins the new invariant across the full route x state matrix, the way the h1 invariant is pinned: the skip link still targets #main, and main#main carries tabindex="-1". The assertions must be genuinely order- and insertion-independent: extract the tag once (/<main([^>]*)>/ and /<a([^>]*)>/) and assert /\bid="main"/ and /\btabindex="-1"/ against the captured attribute string, the shape already used by the .page-title coupling test at test/web/pages.test.js:1091-1093. Asserting the two attributes in one regex with `[^>]*` between them is not enough — it tolerates a third attribute but still fails on <main tabindex="-1" id="main">, which is a valid no-op refactor and would be reverted as a false regression. Pin that property explicitly, as the h1 matcher test at test/web/pages.test.js:145-152 does.

5. A second new test pins the stylesheet rule, matching /#main:focus\s*\{([^}]*)\}/ and asserting outline: none. This follows the precedent set two tickets ago for the .page-title rule at test/web/pages.test.js:1096-1102: asserting the stylesheet's own contents is convention-clean under .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md and it makes AC-3's claim machine-checkable. Without it, the one line that suppresses a visible artefact can be deleted with a green suite.

I applied edits 1-3 locally and re-drove headless Chromium: activeElement becomes MAIN#main on all 25 route x state combinations, and the next Tab enters main on every shell that has a control there. Everything is reverted; the working tree is clean apart from this plan.

files.change: Line 77: `<main id="main">` becomes `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">` in layout(). The landmark is the skip link's target; without tabindex it is not focusable and the link only scrolls. Nothing else in layout() changes, and the emitted attribute is static markup, not user or store data, so it crosses no escaping boundary.
files.why: The root cause. One attribute, no JavaScript, native behaviour in every browser.

files.change: Add a scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }` rule with a comment, placed immediately above the existing `#main { max-width: 1100px; ... }` rule it belongs with. The comment must record two things: that the rule exists because focusing the whole main container paints the global accent ring around the entire 1100px box, which reads as two stray bars at the viewport edges; and that the suppression works by ID specificity (1,1,0 beating the bare `:focus-visible` at 0,1,0 on line 55), so lowering the selector to `main:focus` would silently lose it. `.skip-link:focus` (line 50) and the global `:focus-visible` rule (line 55) are untouched.
files.why: Verified in Chromium: with only the tabindex, main#main matches :focus-visible after activation and the global ring is painted around the whole container. The ring on a landmark communicates nothing a sighted user can act on; the skip link already showed its own visible focus at the moment of activation.

(b) A new test after the heading-hierarchy test, `the skip link targets a focusable main landmark on every route and state`, loops the same ROUTES x STATES matrix and asserts the skip link carries class skip-link and href="#main" and the main landmark carries id="main" and tabindex="-1", each asserted against the tag's captured attribute string so attribute order and any future attribute cannot break it. All probe edits (src/web/pages.js, src/web/styles.css) are reverted, the dev server is stopped and its database removed; `git status --short` shows only the untracked plan/ directory.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add a click handler in src/web/client.js that preventDefaults the skip link and calls document.getElementById('main').focus().
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Strictly worse for the same outcome. It makes the bypass depend on the deferred script having loaded and executed, so the failure mode returns on any slow parse, any CSP change, or a browser that blocks the script; the link would again silently only scroll. It needs preventDefault to suppress the browser's own fragment handling, so it also has to reproduce scrolling by hand, and it adds a second place that knows about the main landmark. The native remedy — tabindex="-1" on the target — is what the HTML spec already prescribes for fragment links to non-focusable targets, works before hydration, and is one attribute.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add the tabindex only, and leave the focus ring the browser paints around main.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is functional but visibly wrong, and I would rather not ship it. Chromium paints the repository's global 2px accent ring around the entire 1100px main container, which at these scroll positions reads as two unexplained vertical bars at the edges of the viewport. Nobody reads that as 'you are in main'. The scoped `#main:focus { outline: none; }` rule is the one extra line that avoids shipping it, and it is the same thing GOV.UK's template does for its skip target. This is a judgement call, not a correctness one — a reviewer who prefers the visible ring can drop the rule without touching the fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Point the skip link at the page's <h1 data-testid="page-title"> instead of at <main>, and give the h1 tabindex="-1".
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Focus would land on a heading, not on the content region, so the bypass lands mid-landmark: screen reader users would hear the page title rather than main, and the next Tab would resume from inside the heading rather than from the top of the content. It also couples the bypass target to a styling-driven element that #46 and #51 have just spent two tickets decoupling from its class. No benefit to trade for that.

alternatives_considered.approach: Handle the wrap-around case at the same time, by making focus land on the first focusable element inside main when one exists.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The wrap is not a defect in the skip link. The shells that wrap contain no focusable element at all — the loading shells are skeletonRows, and the ideal and empty shells on three routes render panels and copy — so there is genuinely nothing for focus to reach, and wrapping to the top of the document is the correct behaviour when the next tab stop is behind you. Fixing it would mean changing page content, which is a product decision belonging in its own ticket. It is stated precisely in residual_risks rather than folded in here.

alternatives_considered.approach: Assert the new invariant with a single regex over the tag, e.g. /<main id="main"[^>]*tabindex="-1"/.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It reads as attribute-order independent and is not. `[^>]*` tolerates a third attribute interleaved between the two asserted ones but still fails on <main tabindex="-1" id="main"> — the same valid markup, emitted in the other order. A no-op refactor would then fail the regression lock and get reverted as a false regression, which is the exact trap the H1_HOOK matcher at test/web/pages.test.js:20-23 exists to avoid, and the currency #44 and #51 were filed to close. The assertions go against the captured attribute string instead, and the property is pinned explicitly.

assumptions: Chromium's behaviour on fragment navigation to a tabindex="-1" target is representative of the browsers QA drives. The spec rule is engine-independent and the technique is long-established, but I verified one engine only.

The route's debug stage will not conclude differently from this. Both the proposal and the critique reproduced the failure on the same tree, and so did I, so a disagreement at debug would be about the remedy rather than the fact of the bug.

docs/ui.md line 114 ('Every page is fully operable by keyboard: visible focus ring, logical tab order matching the region order') is a statement of intent that a landmark container is not a 'user interface component' for focus-ring purposes, so #main:focus needs no ring. This is the premise of the one CSS line; if a reviewer reads 2.4.7 more strictly, that line should be dropped and the bars accepted.

No test other than test/web/pages.test.js:116 depends on the exact text of the <main> tag. This is load-bearing — it is why edit 1 is expected to break exactly one test — and I did not take it on the grep alone: I applied the change and ran the suite, which produced exactly one failure, at that test. The grep and the run agree.

The focusable-element inventory in residual_risks holds for a seeded database, which is the state the QA script sets up. On an unseeded database the ideal states collapse toward the empty shells and the wrap set shifts. It is stated as a property of the shells that have no focusable content, not as a permanent route list, so it survives a reseed.
unknowns: Whether Firefox and WebKit are available anywhere in this pipeline. If QA only ever drives Chromium, the multi-engine gap never closes and AC-1/AC-2 rest on the spec plus Chromium.

Whether the pipeline's browser QA can disable scripting, so that the 'works before hydration' claim in alternatives_considered can actually be exercised. I tried and did not manage it, so the claim stands on the spec rather than on a measurement.

Whether re-activating the skip link in a document whose location.hash is already #main re-runs the focus fixup. Engine-dependent and unmeasured; it is a qa_script step rather than an acceptance criterion because I do not know the right answer to assert.

Whether focusing main#main actually announces the main landmark in a screen reader. This is the user benefit the change exists for and nothing in this pipeline can confirm it; the criteria here are all activeElement- and computed-style-based, and the announcement is carried in residual_risks rather than asserted.

Whether the Librarian intends .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md to record tabindex="-1" as part of the main#main hook contract. The existing line is still true as written, so nothing is broken either way, and that file is one this ticket may not change.
approved_work_order.debate_summary: The council did not agree, and the disagreement was worth having. Both documents agree on the diagnosis and on the remedy, and I confirmed both myself on the running app: tabindex="-1" on the landmark is the right fix, minimal, and its collateral damage is exactly the one test both documents name. Nothing argued for a different fix and I rejected none of the critique's substantive points. What the critique got right, and what changed the work order: the entire verification surface needed rewriting, not the plan's substance. Its two blocking findings both survived my own re-measurement. The error-state one is real and worse than a wording problem — src/web/client.js focuses the retry button inside main on load, so on all five error routes the proposal's 'press Tab once, press Enter' cannot be executed, and the workaround the proposal offered for exactly that case (two Tabs) does not work either. I checked the focus inventory route by route and state by state rather than accepting the critique's list, which is right in direction but still omits the two partial shells; the measured set is in residual_risks and AC-2 is scoped to the shells that actually have something to reach. On its own the critique called AC-2 false for /journal and /experiments in the loading state, which is true and is the case most likely to come back as a bug report after merge. Three further findings I accepted: the new test's advertised attribute-order independence is not achievable with the `[^>]*` technique the proposal prescribes — I confirmed the failure on <main tabindex="-1" id="main">, and the repo's own H1_HOOK precedent says the fix is to assert against the captured tag — the promised 273 is 275 once both new tests land, and I re-confirmed the 273 baseline myself; and the #main:focus rule should be pinned by a test, since this repository added exactly that kind of stylesheet assertion two tickets ago for the .page-title rule and the omission would let the one line that suppresses a visible artefact be deleted with a green suite. Two minor findings I accepted as written (AC-2 named the journal filter select as the landing target for /experiments, which actually lands on INPUT#composer-title; and the CSS comment should record that the suppression works by ID specificity, so nobody later lowers the selector and silently loses it). One finding I recorded as confirmed with no action, since the finding itself asks for none: the caller's grep is exhaustive — my own run of the suite after the change produced exactly one failure, which is the stronger form of that evidence anyway. What I rejected from the critique's edge-case list is the screen-reader criterion: it cannot be passed or failed by anything in this pipeline, so asserting it would buy a criterion nobody can check. It is in residual_risks, where QA will read it and know it is unverified. The proposal's own confidence of 92 was too high for a plan whose acceptance criteria are wrong in two places on 5 and 2 of 25 combinations respectively; mine is 85, and the reasons it is not higher — one engine, an unexercised JavaScript-disabled path, an unmeasured re-activation case, an unverifiable screen-reader claim — are all recorded.
residual_risks: The wrap-around set, measured on a seeded database and re-measured by the arbiter. These shells render no focusable element inside main, so after the skip link moves focus to MAIN#main the next Tab has nothing to reach and returns to the top of the document, where the header is re-entered. The set is: all five routes in the loading state (skeletonRows emits only <div class="skeleton">); / in ideal, empty and partial; /opportunities in ideal and partial; /approvals in ideal and empty. That is 12 of 25 shells, not the three routes the ticket named. QA should go here first, because it is the most likely thing to be reported as a bug after merge. It is correct behaviour given the content, it is a direct improvement on the pre-fix behaviour, and it is deliberately not fixed here — see out_of_scope.
